questions.stem: A 73 year old woman has noticed her right second and third toes turning dark over 6 weeks. She has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 55 years and has calf pain on walking. The toes are black, hard and shrivelled and she says they no longer hurt. There is no discharge or redness. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Black, shrivelled, painless toes with no infection in a heavy smoker with claudication are dry gangrene from chronic arterial insufficiency.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 55 years
steps.x: Chronic ischaemia, mummified toes, no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dry gangrene.

elim: A pigmented patch on the sole or under a nail, not whole shrivelled toes.
Follows trauma, with crepitus, severe pain and systemic toxicity.
Episodic white-blue-red colour change that recovers, not permanent necrosis.
Moist, swollen, painful, infected tissue with pus and fever.

steps.x: **B. Dry gangrene.** Dry, black, shrivelled, painless toes in a smoker = dry gangrene.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 4 day history of a painful, swollen left foot and feeling unwell. His left big toe has been black for 3 weeks. The forefoot is now red, moist and blistered with a foul smell and pus between the toes. Pedal pulses are absent. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Wet gangrene is infection within necrotic tissue: severe pain, erythema, moist blistering, pus, foul odour and fever; it is an emergency.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Necrotic toe plus infection and systemic upset.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wet gangrene.

elim: Spreading skin infection without black necrotic tissue.
Warm, swollen, deformed foot with intact skin and no fever.
Dry, shrivelled, painless and uninfected.
Acute hot joint, not black necrotic tissue with pus.

steps.x: **E. Wet gangrene.** Black + moist + pus + fever = wet gangrene: an emergency.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man cut the sole of his foot on a metal spike while working on a farm 30 hours ago. He now has agonising pain in the foot and calf. The skin around the wound is bronze with bullae and a foul-smelling brown discharge, but there is little redness. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gas gangrene follows a contaminated wound, with pain out of proportion to the signs, bullae, discoloured skin, foul discharge and systemic toxicity.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: cut the sole of his foot
steps.x: Trauma, fast onset, disproportionate pain and a toxic patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gas gangrene.

elim: Red, warm, spreading skin with pain in proportion to signs.
Tense compartment after crush or fracture, no wound discharge or bullae.
A hot, swollen single joint.
Infection of pre-existing ischaemic necrotic tissue, usually in PAD or diabetes.

steps.x: **C. Gas gangrene.** Trauma + pain out of proportion + bullae + foul discharge = gas gangrene.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman had a deep laceration to her calf from a garden fork 2 days ago. She now has severe calf pain, swelling, dusky skin with blisters and crepitus on light palpation. A plain X-ray shows gas in the soft tissues. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 92/60 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is caused by Clostridium perfringens, which produces alpha-toxin and gas in tissue planes.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Soil-contaminated wound with gas in tissue: clostridial myonecrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clostridium perfringens.

elim: An anaerobe in mixed abdominal infections, not the cause of clostridial myonecrosis.
Causes tetanus: muscle spasm and trismus, not myonecrosis with gas.
Causes cellulitis and abscesses, not tissue gas.
Causes necrotising fasciitis and cellulitis; gas is not typical.

steps.x: **B. Clostridium perfringens.** Gas gangrene = Clostridium perfringens.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with peripheral arterial disease has had a darkened left fourth toe for 5 weeks. He smokes and his left ABPI is 0.45. There is no fever, discharge or swelling. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 152/86 mmHg. The vascular registrar suspects dry gangrene.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding in the affected toe?
o: Pink tissue that blanches on pressure
White, waxy tissue that turns red on rewarming
questions.e: Dry gangrene is dry, shrivelled, blackened ('mummified') and painless because the tissue is dead and uninfected.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Ischaemia alone, no infection: the toe mummifies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Painless, shrivelled, black tissue.

elim: Gas gangrene.
Wet gangrene.
Viable, perfused tissue.
Frostbite or Raynaud's.

steps.x: **C. Painless, shrivelled, black tissue.** Dry gangrene = black, shrivelled, mummified, painless.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease has a black right big toe. The surgical team must decide whether this is dry or wet gangrene. There is pus and a foul smell. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which examination finding would most support wet rather than dry gangrene?
o: No clear line between necrotic and healthy tissue
Toe affected rather than the heel
questions.e: Dry gangrene has a clear line of demarcation; in wet gangrene infection spreads so there is no clear line between healthy and necrotic tissue.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Which finding separates the two types?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No clear line between necrotic and healthy tissue.

elim: Occurs in both, as both arise in arterial disease.
Both are black.
A risk factor for both, and not an examination finding.
Both commonly affect the toes.

steps.x: **D. No clear line between necrotic and healthy tissue.** Clear demarcation = dry. No demarcation = wet.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has dry gangrene of his right fifth toe. He drinks 10 units of alcohol a week, has asthma, had varicose veins stripped 20 years ago, and smokes 25 cigarettes a day. His BMI is 24 kg/m². His temperature is 36.5°C and BP 140/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor in his history?
questions.e: Smoking is a specific and major risk factor for dry gangrene through peripheral arterial disease; varicose veins are venous and do not cause gangrene.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Dry gangrene comes from arterial insufficiency; look for the PAD driver.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Smoking.

elim: Within limits and not a key driver.
Not a vascular risk factor.
Normal at 24 kg/m².
Venous disease does not cause ischaemic gangrene.

steps.x: **E. Smoking.** Gangrene risk factors: PVD, diabetes, smoking, arterial thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has two black, dry, painless toes on her left foot with a sharp border. She has had rest pain for 2 months. Her left foot is cold and no pulses are palpable below the femoral. Her temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Gangrene is tissue death from ischaemia; dry gangrene results from chronic arterial insufficiency, usually peripheral arterial disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: no pulses are palpable below the femoral
steps.x: Ischaemia is the cause of tissue death; the pulses tell you why.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Peripheral arterial disease.

elim: Causes venous ulcers, not gangrene.
No history of exposure.
Causes painless ulcers but not tissue death by itself.
Purpura and systemic features; she has absent pulses and risk factors.

steps.x: **C. Peripheral arterial disease.** Gangrene = ischaemic tissue death, usually from PAD.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has wet gangrene of her right foot and has been on the ward for 12 hours. She is confused and has passed little urine. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 80/46 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her blood results?
questions.e: Wet gangrene can cause sepsis and multi-organ failure: hypotension, raised lactate, acute kidney injury and low platelets.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: confused and has passed little urine
steps.x: Infected necrotic tissue, shock and several failing organs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Multi-organ failure from sepsis.

elim: She has not had contrast and it does not explain shock and low platelets.
Ketones are normal.
No vomiting; she is febrile and septic.
Too soon and does not explain shock or low platelets.

steps.x: **D. Multi-organ failure from sepsis.** Gangrene complications: sepsis, multi-organ failure, amputation.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has had painless dry gangrene of his left third toe for 2 months while awaiting vascular review. Over 3 days the toe and surrounding forefoot have become swollen, wet and very painful, with a foul discharge and spreading redness. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg.
questions.q: Which has most likely happened?
questions.e: Necrotic tissue that becomes secondarily infected turns dry gangrene into wet gangrene, which is an emergency.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Dry gangrene that has become wet: what is new is infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection of the necrotic tissue.

elim: Sudden pale, cold, pulseless limb, not pus and fever.
A swollen calf without foul discharge from a toe.
Hot joint without necrotic infected tissue.
Follows revascularisation, which he has not had.

steps.x: **D. Infection of the necrotic tissue.** Dry + infection = wet gangrene.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has an open fracture of his left tibia from a motorbike crash and was treated 36 hours ago. He now has severe leg pain, swelling and bronze skin with bullae around the wound, which has a sweet, foul-smelling discharge. There is crackling under the skin on light touch. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 132 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gas gangrene typically follows trauma and gives bullae, discoloured skin, foul discharge, crepitus and systemic toxicity within hours to days.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: crackling under the skin on light touch
steps.x: Post-traumatic wound with crepitus and shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gas gangrene.

elim: No crepitus or bullae, and not this toxic.
Pain on passive stretch with a tense limb, without crepitus or discharge.
Swollen calf, no wound infection signs.
Develops over weeks, with bone pain rather than crepitus.

steps.x: **D. Gas gangrene.** Crepitus after a contaminated wound = gas gangrene.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease has 3 days of a black, swollen right forefoot. She feels shivery and unwell. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. Her doctors think she has wet gangrene.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the right foot?
o: Absent pulses with moist, blistering black skin
Dry, shrivelled toes that are painless
Tense, shiny, red skin with normal pulses
questions.e: Wet gangrene gives severe pain, erythema, absent pulses and blackish, moist, blistering skin.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Ischaemic limb plus infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Absent pulses with moist, blistering black skin.

elim: She has arterial disease; pulses are absent.
Dry gangrene.
The foot is ischaemic.
Cellulitis or DVT, not gangrene in PAD.

steps.x: **A. Absent pulses with moist, blistering black skin.** Wet gangrene: absent pulses, moist, blistering, black, painful.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has atrial fibrillation and stopped his apixaban 3 months ago. He had a sudden cold, painful right foot 2 weeks ago that he ignored. His right second to fourth toes are now black and dry with a sharp border. There is no discharge. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 98 bpm irregularly irregular.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his gangrene?
questions.e: Arterial thrombosis or embolism (here from AF off anticoagulation) causes ischaemic tissue death; untreated acute ischaemia leaves dry gangrene.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: black and dry with a sharp border
steps.x: AF off anticoagulation, sudden ischaemia, then necrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial thromboembolism.

elim: Causes venous ulcers, not gangrene.
No cold exposure.
Causes painless ulcers, not sudden ischaemia.
Episodic and reversible.

steps.x: **A. Arterial thromboembolism.** Gangrene risk factors include arterial thrombosis as well as PVD, diabetes and smoking.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is admitted with a darkened right big toe. He smokes and has claudication. The surgical registrar must decide which parts of the foot are dead and which are still alive before any further tests. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial assessment?
questions.e: First-line assessment of gangrene is clinical examination to assess tissue viability (colour, warmth, sensation, capillary refill, demarcation), followed by pulses and ABPI.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: which parts of the foot are dead and which are still alive
steps.x: Viability is judged first at the bedside.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical examination of tissue viability.

elim: For occult fracture or osteomyelitis, not viability.
Gold standard to map arteries, done after initial assessment.
For osteomyelitis or deep infection, not the first step.
Invasive and not needed to judge viability.

steps.x: **B. Clinical examination of tissue viability.** Gangrene first-line: clinical examination of viability, then ABPI.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has a black, shrivelled left fifth toe with a clear line of demarcation. She smokes. Investigations: left ankle systolic pressure 80 mmHg, left brachial systolic pressure 145 mmHg. Her temperature is 36.5°C and BP 145/82 mmHg.

visual.title: Left ABPI
visual.caption: Below 0.8: significant arterial disease, supporting dry gangrene.

questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her ABPI?
o: Normal, so another cause must be found
Reduced, supporting dry gangrene from arterial disease
questions.e: ABPI = 80/145 = 0.55; an ABPI below 0.8 shows significant arterial disease and supports dry gangrene.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Work out 80 divided by 145: about 0.55.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reduced, supporting dry gangrene from arterial disease.

elim: That gives an ABPI above 1.3.
Normal is 0.8 or above.
Gas gangrene is an infective diagnosis, not made on ABPI.
ABPI measures arterial, not venous, disease.

steps.x: **D. Reduced, supporting dry gangrene from arterial disease.** ABPI below 0.8 supports dry gangrene.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has dry gangrene of his right second and third toes and rest pain. His right ABPI is 0.4. He is fit for surgery and the vascular team wish to plan revascularisation. His eGFR is 75 mL/min/1.73m². His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the arterial blockage?
questions.e: CT angiography is the gold standard to identify the arterial blockage before revascularisation.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Severity is known; now the anatomy is needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CT angiography.

elim: Looks at veins.
Searches for an embolic source, not the arterial anatomy of the leg.
Shows gas or bone, not arteries.
Already known; does not show where the blockage is.

steps.x: **A. CT angiography.** Gold standard for gangrene's arterial cause = CT angiography.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has severe pain and dusky blistered skin over her forearm 2 days after a deep cut from broken glass. Gas gangrene is suspected. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 90/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Radial pulse is present.
questions.q: Which blood test is most useful to assess the severity of her illness?
questions.e: In suspected gas gangrene, check pulses and ABPI and send bloods including CRP and lactate; lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion and sepsis severity.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
She is shocked: measure hypoperfusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Serum lactate.

elim: For suspected VTE; non-specific here.
Long-term glucose control, not acute severity.
Not relevant.
For myocardial injury, not infection severity.

steps.x: **C. Serum lactate.** Suspected gas gangrene: CRP and lactate.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with diabetes has severe pain in his left thigh 1 day after an intramuscular injection. The skin is bronze with bullae and feels crackly on light palpation. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 94/60 mmHg. A plain X-ray of the thigh is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the X-ray?
o: Gas in the soft tissue planes
questions.e: Gas gangrene shows gas in the soft tissues on imaging, matching crepitus on palpation.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Crepitus means gas, which X-ray shows.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gas in the soft tissue planes.

elim: Suggests tumour or chronic osteomyelitis.
Gas gangrene typically shows gas.
A sign of osteomyelitis developing over weeks.
Seen in chronic conditions, not acute clostridial infection.

steps.x: **A. Gas in the soft tissue planes.** Gas gangrene X-ray: gas in soft tissue planes.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman sees her GP with a black, dry, painless right big toe with a clear line of demarcation. She smokes and has rest pain. There is no fever or discharge. Her right ABPI is 0.42. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Refer to podiatry for routine nail care
questions.e: Dry gangrene needs urgent vascular surgery referral for assessment and revascularisation.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: black, dry, painless right big toe
steps.x: Uninfected dry gangrene with critical ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent referral to vascular surgery.

elim: Worsens arterial ischaemia.
No infection.
The limb is at risk.
Wrong urgency and specialty.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to vascular surgery.** Dry gangrene = urgent vascular referral.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man has dry gangrene of his left third and fourth toes. CT angiography shows diffuse small-vessel disease with no vessel suitable for bypass or angioplasty. The toes are black and clearly non-viable with a clear line of demarcation. He has no fever. His temperature is 36.6°C and BP 142/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the toes?
questions.e: Non-viable tissue is removed by amputation; definitive treatment of gangrene is surgical debridement plus amputation as needed.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: no vessel suitable for bypass or angioplasty
steps.x: Revascularisation is not possible and the tissue is dead.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Amputation of the non-viable toes.

elim: Harmful in arterial disease.
Not a substitute for removing dead tissue.
No infection; antibiotics will not revive dead tissue.
Leaves dead tissue in place at risk of infection.

steps.x: **A. Amputation of the non-viable toes.** Non-viable tissue = amputation.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with diabetes has wet gangrene of her left forefoot with pus and spreading redness. She has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Blood cultures have been taken and the surgical team has been called.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Wet gangrene needs immediate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav (or flucloxacillin plus metronidazole), with urgent surgical review.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Emergency infection in necrotic tissue: IV broad-spectrum cover.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Intravenous co-amoxiclav.

elim: Oral and too narrow for a systemically unwell patient.
Oral and inadequate for wet gangrene.
Used for urinary infection only.
Topical therapy will not treat deep infection.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous co-amoxiclav.** Wet gangrene: IV co-amoxiclav plus urgent surgical review.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has wet gangrene of his right big toe with foul discharge. The hospital antimicrobial policy says co-amoxiclav is not available today. He has no allergies. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg. Surgical review has been requested.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate alternative antibiotic regimen?
o: Intravenous vancomycin alone for 24 hours then review
questions.e: For wet gangrene the alternative to IV co-amoxiclav is IV flucloxacillin plus metronidazole, covering staphylococci, streptococci and anaerobes.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Need IV cover of skin organisms and anaerobes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Intravenous flucloxacillin plus metronidazole.

elim: No anaerobic or Gram-negative cover; not the standard alternative.
Oral, with no anaerobic cover.
Oral and no anaerobic cover.
For urinary infections.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous flucloxacillin plus metronidazole.** Wet gangrene: IV co-amoxiclav, or IV flucloxacillin plus metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with wet gangrene of her left foot has been started on intravenous co-amoxiclav and fluids. There is pus, a foul odour and no clear line of demarcation. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 120/70 mmHg. Her lactate is 2.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation
questions.e: Wet gangrene needs IV antibiotics plus urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation to remove the infected necrotic tissue.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Antibiotics cannot reach dead tissue; source control is needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation.

elim: Worsens ischaemia.
Dead infected tissue must be removed.
She is septic and needs surgery.
Not indicated and adds bleeding risk before surgery.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation.** Wet gangrene: IV antibiotics + urgent debridement/amputation.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has gas gangrene of his right calf after a crush injury 2 days ago. There is crepitus, bullae and severe pain. Gas is seen in the soft tissues on X-ray. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 134 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg. IV fluids are running.
questions.q: Which is the most important step in management?
questions.e: Gas gangrene needs emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue, with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and ICU care.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: Gas is seen in the soft tissues
steps.x: Rapidly spreading myonecrosis: remove the dead muscle now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emergency surgical debridement.

elim: Ignores a life-threatening infection.
At most an adjunct; never instead of surgery.
Oral and not adequate.
Delay is fatal; act on the clinical diagnosis.

steps.x: **B. Emergency surgical debridement.** Gas gangrene = emergency debridement.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with gas gangrene of her left forearm is being prepared for emergency debridement. She has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. The surgeon asks you to start antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Gas gangrene needs IV broad-spectrum antibiotics such as piperacillin-tazobactam (vancomycin or meropenem as alternatives) alongside surgery.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Septic, life-threatening infection: IV broad-spectrum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam.

elim: Oral and too narrow.
Oral, with poor anaerobic and clostridial cover.
Urinary only.
For MRSA decolonisation, not deep infection.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam.** Gas gangrene antibiotics: IV piperacillin-tazobactam.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has had emergency debridement of gas gangrene of his thigh and is on IV piperacillin-tazobactam. Two hours later he is drowsy. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 136 bpm, BP 78/40 mmHg despite 2 litres of IV fluid, and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. Lactate is 7.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Refer to the intensive care unit
questions.e: Gas gangrene is managed with emergency debridement, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and ICU care; he has septic shock needing vasopressors.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.

clues: BP 78/40 mmHg despite 2 litres of IV fluid
steps.x: Fluid-refractory shock after debridement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Refer to the intensive care unit.

elim: He is in septic shock.
He needs organ support.
Does not treat shock.
Irrelevant to shock.

steps.x: **C. Refer to the intensive care unit.** Gas gangrene: debridement + IV antibiotics + ICU.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man had a right second toe amputation for dry gangrene 1 week ago and is recovering well. He has stopped smoking. He takes ramipril and metformin. He has no history of bleeding and is in sinus rhythm. His BP is 132/78 mmHg and total cholesterol is 5.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term medication to add?
questions.e: Underlying vascular disease is treated with an antiplatelet (clopidogrel) and lipid-lowering therapy (atorvastatin).

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the treatment pathway.
Treat the underlying PAD to protect the other toes and heart.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clopidogrel and atorvastatin.

elim: No infection.
No fluid overload.
Impairs healing; no indication.
For AF or VTE; he is in sinus rhythm.

steps.x: **A. Clopidogrel and atorvastatin.** Gangrene from PAD: clopidogrel + atorvastatin long term.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with severe peripheral arterial disease has a black, dry left big toe. CT angiography shows occlusion of the left superficial femoral and tibial arteries. There is no infection. Her temperature is 36.5°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the tissue death?
o: Critically reduced blood supply causing necrosis
questions.e: Dry (ischaemic) gangrene is tissue necrosis from critically reduced arterial blood supply, without infection.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain why the finding in the stem happens.

clues: occlusion of the left superficial femoral and tibial arteries
steps.x: Occluded arteries and no infection: pure ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Critically reduced blood supply causing necrosis.

elim: Wet gangrene.
Gas gangrene.
Frostbite.
Venous ulceration.

steps.x: **C. Critically reduced blood supply causing necrosis.** Dry gangrene = ischaemic necrosis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has dry gangrene of his right fourth toe. The toe is black and hard, and just behind it the skin is pink and warm with a sharp boundary between the two. He smokes. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the skin behind the black toe stays pink?
o: Bacterial gas is held in the necrotic toe
It has been infected and is inflamed
It is still perfused and viable
